# SGDrivE <small>Screwworm Genetic-Control Dynamics Explorer</small>

<!-- badges: start -->
[![Lifecycle: experimental](https://img.shields.io/badge/lifecycle-experimental-orange.svg)](https://lifecycle.r-lib.org/articles/stages.html#experimental)
[![R-CMD-check](https://github.com/prateek1verma/SGDrivE/actions/workflows/R-CMD-check.yaml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/prateek1verma/SGDrivE/actions/workflows/R-CMD-check.yaml)
<!-- badges: end -->

SGDrivE will simulate genotype-resolved population dynamics of the New World
screwworm (*Cochliomyia hominivorax*) under genetic control: the sterile insect
technique (SIT), precision-guided SIT (pgSIT), female-specific RIDL (fsRIDL)
and gene drives.

> **Status: under development (milestone M5, outputs, checks and
> calibration, complete).** The package builds models, solves them
> deterministically (ODE) and stochastically (chain-binomial) with compiled
> C++ solvers checked against pure-R reference solvers and the legacy
> Gutierrez & Ponti (2014) model, and provides output tables, plots, model
> checks and calibration. Scientific validation follows in milestone M6. Do
> not use it for analysis yet.

## Planned model (v0.1)

| Component | Basis |
|---|---|
| Life history: degree-day development, temperature-dependent mortality, adult ageing chains, pre-oviposition period, wound-limited oviposition | Gutierrez & Ponti (2014) |
| Genotype inheritance, read from unmodified inheritance cubes | MGDrivE (Sanchez et al. 2020) |
| Mating: unmated → mated females, male availability | MGDrivE2 (Wu et al. 2021), adapted to NWS |
| Solvers: deterministic ODE and stochastic chain-binomial, one shared C++ rate kernel | SGDrivE |

Populations are tracked as counts per node. The full specification is in
[`dev/MODEL_SPEC.md`](dev/MODEL_SPEC.md) and the design decisions in
[`dev/DECISIONS.md`](dev/DECISIONS.md).

## Installation

The repository is private during development. With access:

``` r
# install.packages("remotes")
remotes::install_github("prateek1verma/SGDrivE")
```

A C++17 compiler is required (Xcode command line tools on macOS, Rtools on
Windows).

## Check the installation

```{r example}
library(SGDrivE)
sg_backend_info()
```

## Building a model (milestone M1)

```{r model, eval = requireNamespace("MGDrivE", quietly = TRUE)}
# parameters (definitions: sg_param_table())
p <- sg_params()
# any MGDrivE inheritance cube
cube <- sg_cube(MGDrivE::cubeMendelian())
# daily forcing from the bundled McAllen, Texas weather
wx <- sg_forcing(sg_example_weather(), p, start = "1971-01-01", end = "1972-12-31")
# weekly releases of 500 adult males of genotype aa
rel <- sg_releases("aa", "adult", "male", times = seq(60, by = 7, length.out = 20), number = 500)
mod <- sg_model(p, cube, wx, rel, area = 1)
mod
```

## Deterministic simulation (milestones M2 and M3)

```{r simulate, eval = requireNamespace("MGDrivE", quietly = TRUE)}
sim <- simulate_ode(mod) # compiled C++ solver (default)
sim
```

`simulate_ode()` integrates the model one day at a time with a Dormand-Prince
5(4) integrator written in C++. A day on which the integrator detects
stiffness is redone with `deSolve`'s `lsoda`. With the defaults and McAllen
weather that has not happened on any day of 24 years.
`simulate_ode(mod, backend = "R")` runs the pure-R reference solver instead:
it gives the same results, 12 to 70 times more slowly.

Both solvers reproduce the legacy Gutierrez & Ponti (2014) ODE (one wild
genotype, `"gp2014"` preset) to a relative error below 10^-6 over 1960-1983
at McAllen, Texas. The C++ solver takes about 4.5 s for those 24 years, and
about 1 s for 24 years of a two-genotype sterile-male release model
(benchmarks in [`bench/`](bench/README.md)).

## Stochastic simulation (milestone M4)

Counts are whole individuals per node, so the node area matters: with the
defaults (1 km^2, 5 wounds per km^2) a McAllen population falls below one
individual in most winters. Here a 1000 km^2 node starts from a one-year
burn-in of the ODE over the weather before the start date:

```{r stochastic, eval = requireNamespace("MGDrivE", quietly = TRUE)}
mod_1000 <- sg_model(p, cube, wx, rel, area = 1000)
init <- sg_init(mod_1000, "burn_in", weather = sg_example_weather())
sim_cb <- simulate_cb(mod_1000, init, n_rep = 10, seed = 1, keep = "totals")
sim_cb
```

`simulate_cb()` divides each day into steps (0.1 day by default). Within a
step, individuals move along their sub-stage chains with the exact
probabilities of the chain over the step, die, mate, lay eggs and emerge, with
binomial, multinomial and Poisson draws; eggs are laid in batches, as egg
masses, by default. The mean of a step is within about 0.5% of the ODE.
Each replicate has its own random-number stream, so it is the same whether
it runs alone, among others or in parallel (`parallel = TRUE`). A two-genotype
release model takes about 0.06 s per simulated year and replicate, nearly
independent of the number of individuals. `extinct_day` and
`wild_extinct_day` report when the population, or its wild type, is gone.

For constant-temperature scenarios, `sg_init(model, "equilibrium",
temperature = 27)` gives the closed-form equilibrium of a wild-type
population.

## Outputs, plots, checks and calibration (milestone M5)

`check_model()` reports a model's size, its fastest processes, the season in
which a wild population can grow (R0, eggs per egg at low density, from
`sg_r0()`), configuration problems and, for stochastic runs, whether the
population is large enough to persist:

```{r check, eval = requireNamespace("MGDrivE", quietly = TRUE)}
check_model(mod_1000)
```

The wound density sets the population size. `calibrate_H()` finds the
density that gives a target, by default the mean adult density over the
model's forcing period:

```{r calibrate, eval = requireNamespace("MGDrivE", quietly = TRUE)}
wx_1971 <- sg_forcing(sg_example_weather(), p, start = "1971-01-01", end = "1971-12-31")
cal <- calibrate_H(sg_model(p, cube, wx_1971), target = 100) # adults per km^2
cal
```

Output tables work the same for deterministic and stochastic results:
`sg_totals()` (by stage, sex, genotype and mate), `sg_allele_freq()`,
`sg_females()` (including females weighted by the fertility of their mate)
and `sg_cases()`, the case proxy: wounds newly infested with viable eggs, so
that females mated to sterile males cause no cases.

```{r outputs, eval = requireNamespace("MGDrivE", quietly = TRUE)}
head(sg_cases(sim, period = "month", host_density = 20))
```

`plot()` draws any of these with ggplot2 in colour-blind-friendly colours;
stochastic replicates are separate lines:

```{r plot, fig.height = 3.5, eval = requireNamespace("MGDrivE", quietly = TRUE) && requireNamespace("ggplot2", quietly = TRUE)}
plot(sim_cb, "cases", period = "month")
```

The McAllen cold-stress index reproduces the values published by Gutierrez &
Ponti (2014) and Gutierrez et al. (2019):

```{r cold}
ci <- sg_cold_index(sg_example_weather())
ci[ci$year %in% c(1971, 1979), c("year", "mu_cold")]
```

## Roadmap

| Milestone | Content |
|---|---|
| M0 ✔ | Foundations: package skeleton, tests, linting, CI, design documents |
| M1 ✔ | Inputs: parameters, inheritance cubes, weather forcing, releases, model assembly |
| M2 ✔ | Reference genotype-resolved ODE in pure R |
| M3 ✔ | C++ rate kernel and ODE solver |
| M4 ✔ | C++ chain-binomial stochastic solver |
| M5 ✔ | Checks, summaries, calibration and plots |
| M6 | Scientific validation |
| M7 | Documentation and v0.1.0 release |

See [`dev/ROADMAP.md`](dev/ROADMAP.md) for completion criteria.

## References

Gutierrez, A.P. & Ponti, L. (2014). The new world screwworm: prospective
distribution and role of weather in eradication. *Agricultural and Forest
Entomology* 16:158–173. <https://doi.org/10.1111/afe.12046>

Sanchez C., H.M., Wu, S.L., Bennett, J.B. & Marshall, J.M. (2020). MGDrivE: A
modular simulation framework for the spread of gene drives through spatially
explicit mosquito populations. *Methods in Ecology and Evolution* 11:229–239.
<https://doi.org/10.1111/2041-210X.13318>

Wu, S.L. et al. (2021). MGDrivE 2: A simulation framework for gene drive
systems incorporating seasonality and epidemiological dynamics. *PLoS
Computational Biology* 17(5):e1009030.
<https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pcbi.1009030>
